On air 3:33 a.m.Channel 0 · Sound department

Recording script

Everything to record for SIGN-OFF's fighters: how each one sounds, every take to cut, the lines they say before a match, and the hits. Tick off takes as you go; your ticks stay in this browser.

7 voices283 files in all45 hit takes, sharedWAV · 48 kHz · mono
DaleRoxHollisMumblesMargaretGusGideonHits

The session

Nothing has to be recorded all at once. Every sound in the game keeps its current stand-in until a recording replaces it, and one good take of a sound is enough to start. One fighter on a Sunday afternoon is a real step forward.

The room

Small and soft: a closet full of clothes beats a big empty room. Fans, fridge and phones off.

The mic

Any decent USB or XLR mic, with a pop filter. A dynamic mic (an SM58 type) forgives an untreated room and loud screams.

Distance and level

A hand's width to 20 cm for speech and efforts; lean back to arm's length for screams. Speech peaking around −10 dB, never touching 0: a clipped take can't be saved, a quiet one can.

The files

48 kHz, 24-bit (16 is fine), mono WAV. One take per file, named as in the tables, in a folder per fighter. No EQ, compression, reverb or trimming: that's all done afterwards.

Performing the efforts

Efforts and pain matter most and are the hardest part. They aren't words: they're the sound of a body working.

  • Move while you do them. Throw a real punch at the air on a heavy effort, push against a wall on a shout, have someone poke you in the ribs for light pain. A still body sounds like reading.
  • Keep them short. A new sound cuts the last one off in the game, so long tails get lost anyway. Lengths are in the tables.
  • Light versus heavy is effort, not volume. A light effort is a breath pushed out, “hp!”; a heavy one comes from the gut, “HAAH!”.
  • Shouts can be words: one short phrase in character (ideas under each fighter), or a pure yell.
  • Pain is surprise first: the breath knocked out, then the voice. The scream is the K.O., the one time everyone loses control.
  • Record extra and keep the best. Two or three times the takes asked for. Variety matters more than polish: the game never plays the same take twice in a row, so takes that differ a little are what make it sound alive.

The _N in a file name is the take number: effort_heavy_1.wav, effort_heavy_2.wav, effort_heavy_3.wav.

The cast

Seven people the channel caught, or made. Each section has how they sound, then every file to record for them.

Hits and foley

Shared by everyone, in a folder called hits/. Each hit file is one layer, not a finished punch: the game stacks layers by how hard the hit lands. A jab is a snap and a thud; a launcher is a snap, a thud, a crunch and a boom. So keep each one to its own job.

Free libraries

  • Sonniss GDC bundles (sonniss.com/gameaudiogdc): free, royalty-free, commercial use allowed. Search punch, body impact, bodyfall, whoosh, cloth.
  • Freesound (freesound.org): filter by licence. CC0 needs nothing, CC-BY needs a credit, skip anything marked NC.
  • Kenney (kenney.nl): CC0, a small impact pack.

Paid

A Sound Effect (asoundeffect.com) has many punch and fighting libraries; BOOM Library and Soundly are the professional end.

Note where every library sound came from and its licence.

Make your own

  • Punch a leather jacket or a couch cushion: thud.
  • Snap celery, twist a cabbage: crunch.
  • Slap a forearm on a padded surface: block.
  • Drop a duffel bag of clothes: bodyfall.
  • Swing a thin stick or a belt past the mic: whoosh.
  • A real frying pan, a knife on a steel, a broom handle on a table: metal, blade, wood.

Sending the files

  • One folder per fighter, named as in the slates (dale/, rox/, mumbles/…), plus hits/.
  • File names exactly as in the tables, lower case, ending .wav. A misspelled name is caught and turned away, so nothing breaks; it just won't play until it's renamed.
  • Untouched takes: the trimming, levels and conversion happen on the way into the game.
  • Voice actors: before recording, agree in writing that the recordings can be used in SIGN-OFF, in any form, on any platform, for good.

Stand-ins in the meantime

Text-to-sound and voice-design tools can fill gaps while waiting for real recordings, which is fine for trying a character's voice out. Non-verbal efforts and pain are hit and miss, the terms differ by plan and need reading before anything ships, and a real person's voice is never cloned.
